property_summary: For every caller/context where proxiableUUID() is called on the implementation contract, the correct contract returns the canonical ERC1967 implementation slot (ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT); the mutant returns a different value (bytes32(0)) for some inputs, so the returned UUID will differ.

For any caller context where proxiableUUID() completes, the reference C always returns ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT while the mutant returns a different bytes32 for at least some caller contexts; thus calling proxiableUUID() and comparing its return to ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT must always be true on the reference but can be false on the mutant for some fuzzed caller (address) and call context (EOA vs contract), so the property is that proxiableUUID() == ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT for all callers.

For every caller context that successfully calls C.proxiableUUID(), the correct contract returns ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT; the mutant returns a different bytes32 (bytes32(0)) for some callers, so there exists a caller for which proxiableUUID() != ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT.

After initialize(...) completes, the contract's UUPS proxiableUUID() must be callable in non-delegated context (i.e. initialize on reference calls __UUPSUpgradeable_init so proxiableUUID() can be called notDelegated and return IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT; the mutant omits that initialization causing proxiableUUID() to revert in some contexts), so for any admin address the reference returns the implementation slot via proxiableUUID when called directly, while the mutant will cause a revert for some fuzzed caller/address scenario.

After initialize(...) the reference contract always allows calling proxiableUUID() in non-delegated context (it will return the ERC1967 IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT) for any caller, whereas the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() causes proxiableUUID() to revert for at least some callers due to the notDelegated / __self check failing; the test fuzzes a caller address and asserts that calling proxiableUUID() from that caller does not revert.

After initialize(...) succeeds, calling upgradeToAndCall(...) (which requires onlyProxy and thus checks ERC1967 implementation slot is set to this contract via __UUPSUpgradeable_init) must revert when not a proxy; the reference initializes UUPS so subsequent direct calls to proxiableUUID() are allowed (notDelegated) while the mutant leaves __self check such that calling proxiableUUID() via a delegatecall-like context (simulated by using a helper that delegatecalls into C) behaves differently; specifically, for any fuzzed helper caller bytecode selector, the reference preserves notDelegated semantics preventing delegatecall success while the mutant allows a delegatecall path to report a different outcome — the test asserts that delegatecall to proxiableUUID() reverts (ok == false) for all helper-caller code hashes the fuzzer tries, which the buggy version will fail for some input.

For any caller address and any accessControl address, calling initialize(...) on C should always complete successfully (not revert) and leave the contract in a state where calling proxiableUUID() via a direct call from the deployer (not via delegatecall) does NOT revert; the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() causes proxiableUUID() to revert when invoked in certain call contexts, so there exists fuzzed caller input for which proxiableUUID() reverts after initialize on the mutant but not on the reference.

After initialize(...) returns successfully, calling proxiableUUID() via a direct external call from the contract itself (i.e. address(c).call with the proxiableUUID selector) must not revert for any fuzzed caller-supplied target address used to perform an external CALL into c; the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() leaves __self check such that an external low-level CALL from a contract whose address equals c (simulated via a helper that performs a CALL into c using the provided caller address as its tx.origin) can cause proxiableUUID() to revert for some helper deployment bytecode/caller combination — the reference never reverts in this scenario while the mutant does for some inputs.

After calling initialize(...) once from any account, the contract's Initializable_storage._initialized equals 1 (reference) for all inputs, but the mutant sets it to 2 causing the stored initialized version to differ for some inputs.

After calling initialize(...) the reference always allows a subsequent reinitializer(version=2) call (i.e. initialize sets stored initialized to 1 so reinitializer(2) succeeds), whereas the mutant that sets initialized to 2 in initializer blocks reinitializer(2) (it will revert); the test asserts that calling initialize(...) does not prevent a later reinitializer(2) call from succeeding.

For any caller and any accessControl address, calling initialize(...) on the correct contract always returns (does not revert) and emits Initialized(1) while leaving the contract callable by initialize once (i.e., initialize is accepted as a top-level initializer that sets initialized to 1), whereas the mutant changes the stored initialized to 2 causing initialize() to still succeed but the emitted Initialized event's argument remains 1 in reference but the mutant also emits 1 — instead, we assert that after initialize() completes, a subsequent call to proxiableUUID() with notDelegated context (i.e., calling the function directly on the implementation, not via delegatecall) must revert under the reference but may behave differently under the mutant; to robustly distinguish, we check that calling proxiableUUID() directly on the implementation (not via delegatecall) reverts with UUPSUnauthorizedCallContext under the reference for all inputs, and the mutant may allow it (i.e., not revert) for some inputs.

For any caller and any accessControl address, calling initialize(...) on the correct implementation always returns (does not revert) and leaves the contract callable such that a subsequent direct call to proxiableUUID() (not via delegatecall) still reverts with UUPSUnauthorizedCallContext; the mutant that sets _initialized = 2 in initializer can make the post-initialize direct proxiableUUID() call succeed (not revert) for some inputs, so the property is that proxiableUUID() called directly on the implementation must always revert after initialize(...) completes.

For every caller and accessControl address, calling initialize(...) on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert) and leaves the contract in a state where a subsequent call to proxiableUUID() made directly on the implementation (i.e. not via delegatecall) still reverts with UUPSUnauthorizedCallContext; the mutant that sets _initialized = 2 in initializer can allow proxiableUUID() to succeed (not revert) for some inputs, breaking this rule.

For any call to rate, when block.timestamp > utilizationData.lastUpdate the contract MUST compute utilization from IVault.currentUtilizationIndex and elapsed/time-delta path (updating index and lastUpdate); the mutant inverts the condition and therefore for some lastUpdate/timestamp values it will choose the wrong branch and return a different latestAnswer.

For any vault/asset state and timestamp, if block.timestamp > utilizationData.lastUpdate then calling rate updates utilizationData.index/lastUpdate and returns a value computed from the index/elapsed path; the mutant inverts the condition and therefore for some fuzzed lastUpdate/timestamp inputs the mutant will choose the wrong branch and return a different latestAnswer.

For any vault, asset and utilization storage where block.timestamp > utilizationData.lastUpdate, calling rate(...) updates utilizationData.index/lastUpdate and returns the value computed from the index/elapsed branch; the mutant inverts the timestamp check and can choose the wrong branch (returning a different latestAnswer) when block.timestamp > lastUpdate.

For any vault/asset and any lastUpdate <= block.timestamp, calling rate(...) on the reference will take the elapsed/index path (updating index and lastUpdate) and return a value consistent with that branch; the mutant inverts the timestamp check and therefore for some fuzzed lastUpdate and block.timestamp values will choose the wrong branch and return a different latestAnswer.

For any vault/asset and any starting utilization storage, if block.timestamp > utilizationData.lastUpdate then C.rate(...) will take the elapsed/index branch (updating index and lastUpdate) and return the value computed from that branch; the mutant inverts the timestamp check so for some fuzzed lastUpdate and block.timestamp values it will take the wrong branch and return a different latestAnswer.

For any call to rate(_vault,_asset), if block.timestamp > utilizationData.lastUpdate then the returned latestAnswer must equal _applySlopes(...) computed with a non-zero elapsed when IVault.currentUtilizationIndex returns a different index than utilizationData.index (i.e., when index != utilizationData.index), but the mutant that forces elapsed=0 can make rate(...) differ when index != utilizationData.index.

If the vault's currentUtilizationIndex changes since the stored index (index != utilizationData.index) and block.timestamp > lastUpdate, the reference computes utilization using a non-zero elapsed and returns a rate equal to calling rate twice with same inputs (idempotent across repeated calls when time and external index unchanged); the mutant that zeroes elapsed can produce a different returned rate in that scenario.

For any vault/asset and current block time, if the vault's reported currentUtilizationIndex equals the stored utilization index (so IVault.currentUtilizationIndex(_asset) == utilizationData.index), calling rate does not rely on elapsed-from-index and both reference and mutant return the same value; the bug (forcing elapsed=0) breaks this when the index has advanced since lastUpdate and elapsed would otherwise be nonzero — so we assert that when index == stored index the returned rate is stable (both compute via IVault.utilization path) for all inputs, and the mutant will differ for some inputs where index != stored index, but our admissible domain restricts to index == stored index to ensure reference holds for all fuzz inputs while mutant can still be distinguished elsewhere by fuzzer across runs.

For any vault/asset and any timestamps, if the vault's currentUtilizationIndex equals the stored utilization index (so no index-change-based division by elapsed is needed), then calling rate(...) always returns the same value for the reference and does not revert; the mutant that zeroes elapsed can still differ when the index has changed, but by restricting inputs to cases where IVault.currentUtilizationIndex(...) == stored index the reference always succeeds and returns the same value while the mutant will remain indistinguishable for these admissible inputs (thus the reference's property holds universally for the admissible domain).

For any vault, asset, and prior stored utilization index, if the vault's currentUtilizationIndex(_asset) equals the stored utilization index and block.timestamp is not less than lastUpdate, then calling rate(_vault,_asset) always returns the same value on the correct contract (it uses IVault.utilization path) — the mutant that forces elapsed=0 can still change behavior when the index differs, so the rule targets the case where index == stored index which the reference always preserves for all fuzz inputs but the mutant can break for other inputs.

For any vault, asset and on-chain time, calling rate(...) when block.timestamp > stored lastUpdate updates storage.index from the freshly-read IVault.currentUtilizationIndex before calling _applySlopes so the computed utilization uses that index; the mutant that assigns lastUpdate before index can change elapsed/index relationship and thus produce a different returned latestAnswer for some inputs.

For any vault/asset/timestamp where block.timestamp > stored lastUpdate, C.rate updates storage.index to the freshly-read IVault.currentUtilizationIndex before calling _applySlopes so the computed utilization uses that index (the mutant that sets lastUpdate before index can cause _applySlopes to observe inconsistent elapsed/index and thus return a different latestAnswer for some inputs).

For any vault, asset and timestamp where block.timestamp > stored lastUpdate, calling rate(...) on the correct contract preserves the freshly-read currentUtilizationIndex in storage before calling into _applySlopes (so returned latestAnswer is consistent with index computed from currentUtilizationIndex), while the mutant that assigns lastUpdate before index can change the observed elapsed/index relation and thus produce a different latestAnswer for some fuzzed inputs.

For any vault/asset/timestamp where block.timestamp > stored lastUpdate, calling rate(...) on the correct contract updates storage.index to the freshly-read IVault.currentUtilizationIndex before returning and thus subsequent call to rate with same inputs yields a deterministic relationship: calling rate twice in a row without intervening external changes yields the same returned latestAnswer from the reference, whereas the mutant (which sets lastUpdate before index) can cause the second call to return a different latestAnswer for some fuzzed inputs.

For any vault/asset and starting stored utilization index/lastUpdate, calling rate(...) twice in succession (without external state changes) on the correct contract yields the same returned latestAnswer on both calls, whereas the mutant that swaps assigning lastUpdate and index can make the two calls return different values for some fuzzed inputs.

For any supplied SlopeData, the reference contract always rejects any kink equal to 0 or >= 1e27 (i.e. setSlopes reverts when kink == 0 or kink >= 1e27), while the mutant accepts kink == 0 (only rejects kink >= 1e27) — therefore for some fuzzed kink == 0 the reference will revert but the mutant will succeed, distinguishing them.

For every input slopes.kink the reference C rejects (reverts) when kink == 0 or kink >= 1e27, whereas the mutant accepts kink == 0 (only rejects kink >= 1e27); thus the invariant: calling setSlopes with kink == 0 must revert on the reference but the mutant will sometimes succeed, distinguishing them.

For all inputs, the reference C always REVERTS when setSlopes is called with _slopes.kink equal to the storage default (zero) after deployment because it disallows kink==0; the mutant (which allows kink==0) will sometimes accept and store a kink of 0 — thus the property: calling setSlopes with a freshly zero-initialized SlopeData.kink must revert on the correct contract but not on the buggy one for some fuzzed inputs.

For every fuzzed input slopes, the reference C always REVERTS when setSlopes is called with _slopes.kink == 0, whereas the mutant (which removed the kink==0 rejection) will accept (succeed) for some inputs — so calling setSlopes with kink==0 must revert on the correct contract but may succeed on the buggy one.

For all inputs, calling setSlopes with a SlopeData whose kink is zero must revert on the correct contract (P) because P forbids kink==0, while the mutant (M) removes that check and will accept kink==0 for some inputs, so the property is that setSlopes reverts when kink==0 on the reference.

For any kink value the reference contract accepts (i.e., any uint256 kink where setSlopes does not revert), calling setSlopes stores that kink in the contract and returns normally; the mutant inverts the check and will revert for many previously-acceptable kink inputs (some kink < 1e27), so there exist fuzzed inputs where the reference accepts but the mutant rejects.

For all input slope structs with kink in (0, 1e27) the reference contract accepts setSlopes (does not revert) and stores the slopes; the mutant inverts the check and will revert for some such kinks, so there exist fuzzed inputs where reference succeeds but mutant reverts.

For every input slopes struct with kink in (0, 1e27) the reference C accepts setSlopes (call succeeds) while the mutant rejects (call reverts), so the general rule: setSlopes should succeed for any 0 < kink < 1e27; the bug inverts that check and causes reverts for these kinks.

For any SlopeData with kink in the admissible range (0 < kink < 1e27) the reference C accepts setSlopes (call does not revert); the mutant inverts the validation and will revert for some such kink values, so the property is that setSlopes should succeed for any kink in (0,1e27) and the mutant breaks this by reverting.

For any SlopeData.kink in (0, 1e27) calling setSlopes should succeed (reference C accepts such kinks), whereas the mutant inverts the check and will revert for those kinks, so the property is that setSlopes does not revert for 0 < kink < 1e27 and the mutant breaks this.

For any input slopes, the reference contract always reverts (rejects) when kink is 0 or >= 1e27, but the mutant accepts such invalid kink values (so a call that should revert succeeds for some fuzz inputs).

For all inputs, the reference C rejects (reverts) any setSlopes call whose _slopes.kink is 0 or >= 1e27, but the mutant removes that validation and therefore will accept (succeed) for some such fuzzed kink values.

For every input slopes struct, the reference contract reverts when _slopes.kink is 0 or >= 1e27 while the mutant (which removed the validation) will succeed for some such kink values; thus the property is that calls with kink==0 or kink>=1e27 must revert on the reference and the mutant violates this by sometimes returning success.

For every input slopes struct, the reference contract reverts when _slopes.kink is 0 or >= 1e27, while the mutant (which removed that validation) will sometimes accept such slopes; the property asserts that calls with kink==0 or kink>=1e27 always revert on the reference.

For every input slopes struct where kink is either 0 or >= 1e27, the reference contract always reverts when calling setSlopes (rejecting invalid kink values); the mutant removes that check and will accept (succeed) for some such fuzzed kink values, so the property is that calls with invalid kink must revert on the reference but may succeed on the mutant.

For all callers and slope inputs, the reference contract requires access control to call setSlopes (calls by unauthorized callers revert), whereas the mutant removes this check allowing any caller to successfully set slopes; the test fuzzes caller address and slope.kink to find a caller that is unauthorized in reference but succeeds in mutant.
